input.rationale: Another input path for the proposal side, opened while reviewing how proposals reach a leader: stepLeader unmarshals a proposal's conf-change payload and panics on a decode error (raft.go:1305-1313), while stepFollower forwards a MsgProp to its leader without inspecting the entry payload at all (raft.go:1714-1724) and the forwarded message carries no term (raft.go:536-541), so a malformed conf-change proposal reaches the leader's unmarshal either directly or through a member that believes it is relaying a normal client proposal. One control and two probes measure exactly that, with the panic recovered in the harness so the outcome is reported verbatim.

investigations.question: Does a proposal whose conf-change entry cannot be decoded abort the node that processes it, and does a follower's proposal-forwarding hop validate the payload before relaying it to the leader?
investigations.hypothesis: stepLeader decodes the conf-change payload of a proposal and panics on failure, stepFollower forwards a proposal without examining its entries and without attaching a term, so a proposal carrying an undecodable conf-change payload aborts whichever node decodes it, and relaying it through a follower only moves the abort to the leader without any rejection at the relay.
investigations.discriminator: On a freshly elected three-voter cluster, step a MsgProp carrying an EntryConfChangeV2 whose Data cannot be decoded (a) directly into the leader and (b) into a follower that forwards proposals, recording for each: whether the stepping node panicked and with which recovered text, how many messages the follower produced and to whom, the leader's panic and recovered text for the forwarded case, and the last index before and after. Use a well-formed conf change of the same entry type as the control, which must be appended without aborting. If the malformed proposal is rejected with an error instead of aborting, or if the follower refuses to relay it, the hypothesis is refuted.
limitations: The malformed payload is constructed by the harness as bytes that fail protobuf decoding; it represents a corrupt, truncated or otherwise invalid payload rather than any particular producer.
The probes step messages directly into the state machines; the transport and any application-level validation between peers are outside the captured package.
Only the EntryConfChangeV2 variant is probed directly and through forwarding; the legacy EntryConfChange variant shares the same unmarshal-and-panic shape but was not executed.
Whether reachability through a real peer is within the trusted message contract is a question for human review.

knowledge.statement: In stepLeader, a MsgProp whose entry type is EntryConfChange or EntryConfChangeV2 is unmarshalled into the corresponding conf-change struct and any decode error panics the node processing the proposal (raft.go:1305-1313); nothing earlier on the path inspects the payload, because stepFollower relays a proposal by only rewriting m.To and sending it, without attaching a term or decoding the entries (raft.go:1714-1724 with raft.go:536-541). A proposal carrying an undecodable conf-change payload therefore aborts whichever node decodes it, and the follower that relays it neither rejects nor detects the problem.
knowledge.conditions: The receiver is a leader in the middle of handling MsgProp (for example a freshly elected leader in a three-voter configuration), the proposal is delivered either directly or through a follower that forwards proposals to its leader, and the entry type is a conf-change type with a payload that fails the library's protobuf decode.

scope.description: Three probes on freshly elected three-voter clusters, each stepping one MsgProp carrying an EntryConfChangeV2 into a real state machine with any panic recovered: a malformed payload directly into the leader, the same malformed payload into follower 2 (whose forwarded message is then stepped into the leader), and a well-formed payload directly into the leader as the control.
assumptions: The cluster is built with newNetwork and elected by nt.send(MsgHup), so the leader has a committed entry in its term and the follower knows its leader.
The malformed payload is the byte sequence {0xff,0xff,0xff,0xff}, which the library's protobuf decoding rejects.
Proposals are delivered as pb.Message{Type: MsgProp, Entries: [{Type: EntryConfChangeV2, Data: payload}]}, which is the shape a caller or a forwarding follower produces.
The follower's relayed message is stepped into the leader by the harness, which is the same message the transport would deliver.
Panics are recovered by the harness only; in production the same panic escapes (*raft).Step and aborts the caller's raft loop.
excluded: The transport, admission control and any authentication between peers
The legacy EntryConfChange entry type
Snapshots, membership changes, restarts and joint configurations
Any state-machine effect of the proposal, since the malformed payload never reaches the log

experiment.prefix: Harness (draft file assurance_generated_test.go, package raft, execution package '.'; no captured file is replaced). assuranceCluster-equivalent setup: three real raft instances with newTestRaft(1|2|3, 10, 1, newTestMemoryStorage(withPeers(1,2,3))) wired with newNetwork and elected by nt.send(MsgHup); the harness asserts node 1 is StateLeader, advances its applied index to its committed index and clears the queues. For each probe it emits conf_proposal_setup with probe_id, scenario, via_follower, data_len, leader, term, leader state, committed and applied; it then steps the proposal with assuranceStepRecover, which recovers any panic and reports the verbatim value plus the messages the node produced. For the malformed-direct probe the proposal is stepped into the leader; for the malformed-via-follower probe it is stepped into follower 2 (whose single forwarded MsgProp to node 1 is recorded and then stepped into the leader, with the leader's own panic recovered); for the valid control a marshalled ConfChangeV2 adding node 4 is stepped into the leader. Each probe emits conf_proposal_outcome with probe_id, scenario, via_follower, follower_panicked, follower_recovered, follower_messages, forwarded_to, leader_panicked, recovered, last_index_before, last_index_after and leader state. The harness asserts that the forwarding hop neither panics nor changes the number of forwarded messages, so a failure at the relay cannot be mistaken for the leader's outcome.
experiment.responsibility: The proposal path owns deciding whether a proposal can be turned into log state and reporting a failure to its caller; a payload it cannot decode must be rejected as a proposal rather than converted into an abort of the node that processes it, and a node that relays a proposal owns at least not to propagate a shape it knows the leader will abort on.

comparisons.description: Stepping a proposal with an undecodable conf-change payload directly into a leader does not abort the node.
Relaying the same malformed proposal through a follower does not let it abort the leader that decodes it.
Control: a well-formed conf change of the same entry type is appended without aborting the leader.

investigations.question: On a stable leader using ReadOnlySafe, can a ReadIndex request that carries an rctx equal to one that is still pending complete, or is that request silently discarded so that its requester receives no read index answer while the cluster keeps making progress?
investigations.hypothesis: The leader keys pending read requests by the rctx string only, so a second admission carrying an equal rctx is dropped without recording its own request message; when the single status completes, the answer is addressed to the first admission's requester and no answer is ever produced for the second requester, even though the leader stays leader and keeps satisfying quorum heartbeat acknowledgments.
investigations.discriminator: Drive two real voters to forward ReadIndex messages with equal rctx to the leader before any quorum acknowledgment, then deliver the quorum ack and eight further heartbeat rounds with acks from both followers; count read index answers per requester while confirming the leader stays in StateLeader. Controls: the identical shape with distinct rctxes (both requesters must be answered) and a single requester retrying its own rctx (that requester must be answered), which separate a duplicate-rctx admission loss from a broken harness or a generally stalled leader.

knowledge.assertion: The second admission with an equal rctx is discarded, so the leader keeps exactly one pending status and one stored request message for the two admissions.
Completion answers only the stored first request message, so a discarded equal-rctx admission produces neither a MsgReadIndexResp nor a ReadState.

counterevidence: node.go:218-229 states that callers must not reuse an rctx and that the reuse restriction is only lifted starting with release-3.7, so the silent drop may be the documented behaviour of this release-3.6 revision rather than an implementation error; this draft reports the mechanism and the observed starvation, and leaves that classification to human review.

The same-requester retry case is answered: when one requester retries its own rctx while the status is pending, the single response is addressed to that requester, so the observed starvation requires a requester whose equal-rctx message is discarded because another requester was admitted first.

Existing test coverage (raft_test.go:1192-1222) exercises one unique rctx and only checks that the queue and pending map drain; node_test.go:196-241 forwards two equal rctxes from different nodes but asserts only that the messages are forwarded and never checks for read index answers.
limitations: Only ReadOnlySafe is exercised; ReadOnlyLeaseBased and the pendingReadIndexMessages path (a leader that has not yet committed an entry in its term) are out of scope for this experiment.
The observation window is eight leader heartbeat rounds with quorum acknowledgments in one process; it establishes repeated nonprogress under normal opportunities rather than an unbounded guarantee.
The requester-side application contract (matching ReadStates by RequestCtx) is read from node.go / rawnode.go rather than executed.

investigations.question: Can a MsgReadIndex with an empty Entries slice reach the leader's read-index producer and panic the node, or is the message rejected, dropped or validated before the producer dereferences Entries[0]?
investigations.hypothesis: MsgReadIndex is sent and forwarded without a term (raft.go:536-541 keeps the local-message treatment for MsgProp/MsgReadIndex), a follower forwards it unchanged to its leader while a leader passes it straight to sendMsgReadIndexResponse (raft.go:1759-1765, 1346-1363), and that producer dereferences m.Entries[0] in readOnly.addRequest and responseToReadIndexReq without checking the slice length; only MsgReadIndexResp has an entry-count check (raft.go:1766-1772) and only MsgProp has an explicit empty-entry panic (raft.go:1286-1289). The apparent mismatch is therefore that the same message shape is validated for the response direction and for proposals but not for the request direction entering the leader's producer.
investigations.discriminator: Step a MsgReadIndex carrying no Entries into a follower (expected: forwarded to its leader, raft.go:1759-1765) and into a leader (expected by this hypothesis: an index-out-of-range panic inside the read-index producer), then step a well-formed one-entry MsgReadIndex into the same node as a positive control. Use a recovering wrapper that records the recovered value plus the leader's state, term and readOnly queue/pending sizes at the moment of the panic, and compare with the empty-MsgProp path that panics deliberately. If the empty-Entries message is instead dropped, converted to an error or silently ignored, the hypothesis is refuted and the observed disposition is the finding.

knowledge.assertion: readOnly.addRequest uses m.Entries[0].Data as the request key, which is the unchecked access that aborts on an empty payload.
responseToReadIndexReq answers the stored request through req.Entries[0].Data, so the same unchecked premise exists on the completion path.

limitations: A malformed or forged peer message may be considered outside the trusted transport contract, so a panic here would be an availability/robustness question rather than a divergence from consensus; the question is registered to establish the actual behaviour first.
The discriminator has not been executed yet; the hypothesis is provisional and rests only on the captured dispatch and producer code.
The node-to-transport boundary is not part of the captured package, so reachability through a real peer depends on what the embedding application forwards to Node.Step.

investigations.question: When a conf change proposal fails the leader's propose-time validation, the leader replaces the entry with an empty EntryNormal and appends it while returning no error: can the proposing caller distinguish a discarded configuration change from an accepted one through the proposal result, and what does the log carry instead?
investigations.hypothesis: The conversion at raft.go:1333 keeps the proposal accepted: appendEntry succeeds, the returned error stays nil, the proposed index receives a normal entry with no data, pendingConfIndex is deliberately left untouched so the failed change is not treated as pending, and the resulting ConfState never changes, so a caller that only inspects the proposal result (nil error, committed index) cannot tell that its membership change was dropped. The apparent mismatch is between the proposal API's success signal and the responsibility to establish that the requested configuration change was admitted.
investigations.discriminator: On a leader in a simple (non-joint) configuration, propose a ConfChangeV2 with no changes and record (i) the error returned by Step, (ii) the type and Data length of the entry appended at the proposed index, (iii) the ConfState before and after that entry is committed and applied, and (iv) whether a second conf change proposed while one is pending is converted in the same way. Run the same proposal with DisableConfChangeValidation enabled as the control that must bypass the conversion, and compare with a valid single-node conf change as the positive control that must reach the applied ConfState. If the proposal error or the applied entry type/ConfState turn out to carry the distinction, the hypothesis is refuted.
counterevidence: The conversion is deliberate in the captured source: it is guarded by !r.disableConfChangeValidation, preceded by an Infof line naming the failed check, and Config.DisableConfChangeValidation documents propose-time verification as a feature, so a reviewer may read the empty-normal-entry substitution as intended behaviour rather than a silent drop.

The applying application sees the entry type when it applies the log, so an embedding server can in principle detect that its conf change became a normal entry; the question is about the proposal result and about what the library, not the embedding, guarantees.
limitations: No execution has been run for this question yet; the hypothesis rests only on the captured producer and the configuration documentation.
The discriminator covers a simple configuration and the empty-change case; joint configurations, learner changes and removals are separate branches of the same validation block.
Client-visible membership semantics of an embedding application (for example etcd's conf-change waiters) are outside the captured package.

investigations.question: When a committed configuration change removes the current leader and Config.StepDownOnRemoval is false, does the cluster still reach a new leader, or does the ineligible leader keep the leadership role and its heartbeats reset every eligible voter so that no proposal can commit and no election can complete without external intervention?
investigations.hypothesis: switchToConfig keeps the leadership role for a node that is absent from the new configuration when step-down is not requested, stepLeader then drops every proposal because the leader has no progress entry, and tickHeartbeat keeps broadcasting heartbeats that reset every remaining voter's election timer, so the cluster can neither commit client writes nor elect a replacement; with StepDownOnRemoval=true the same applied change makes the node a follower and the remaining voters elect a new leader.
investigations.discriminator: Propose, replicate and apply a ConfChangeV2 that removes node 1 on a three-voter cluster, then tick every node for a fixed number of rounds with prompt message delivery and record node states, whether a new leader was elected, the last index and committed index, and the proposal errors on the leader and on a forwarding follower; repeat with StepDownOnRemoval=true as the control. Also probe the read path on the ineligible leader with one and then a quorum of acknowledgments from the current voters. If the ineligible leader is eventually replaced, or if the followers campaign despite the heartbeats, the hypothesis is refuted.
limitations: The harness drives timers by ticking each node once per round in a fixed order, which is a legitimate but synthetic schedule; a real deployment also has network and scheduling jitter.
The probe covers simple removal of the leader in a three-voter cluster; joint configurations, learner demotion and multi-node changes are not exercised.
Whether StepDownOnRemoval=false is the right default for an embedding service, and whether an operator is expected to intervene, is a contract question outside the captured package.

investigations.question: When a second ReadIndex request is admitted with an rctx equal to one that is still pending, does the answer produced for that admission carry a read index at least as new as the leader's commit index observed at the second admission, or does it carry the first admission's older index?
investigations.hypothesis: readOnly.addRequest stores the read index only for the first admission with a given rctx (read_only.go:56-63), so a second admission with the same rctx creates no status of its own and the single answer produced on acknowledgment uses the first admission's stored index (raft.go:1596-1606, 2068-2084). If the leader committed an entry between the two admissions, the answer delivered for the later admission is older than that admission's commit index.
investigations.discriminator: On a three-voter cluster, forward ReadIndex with rctx X from follower 2, hold the resulting heartbeats so the status stays pending, commit a write through the real replication path, then admit a second ReadIndex with the same rctx X and deliver the follower acknowledgments; record the commit index at each admission and the index carried by the answer for X. Repeat with distinct rctxes as the control, where the second admission must have its own status and its answer must carry the newer index. If the coalesced answer carries the later index, or if the control behaves the same way, the hypothesis is refuted.

knowledge.assertion: The second admission with an equal rctx keeps exactly one pending status and stores no request message of its own, so no per-admission index exists for it.

limitations: The harness plays the application duties (holding and later delivering messages, and driving the followers' Step calls); no real transport is involved.
Only one interleaving is probed: one write committed between the two admissions in a three-voter cluster with the default ReadOnlySafe.

Whether an embedding application is allowed to reuse an rctx for a distinct read request is a contract question; release-3.6 documentation forbids it while the same comment states the restriction is lifted from release-3.7, so the finding is about the producer's index association, not about an application contract.

investigations.question: Does a ReadIndex request that reaches a leader before it has committed an entry in its current term get delivered once that first commit happens, or can it remain queued while the leader keeps making progress?
investigations.hypothesis: A MsgReadIndex submitted before the leader's first commit in its term is appended to r.pendingReadIndexMessages with no heartbeat broadcast, and the queue is drained only in the MsgAppResp-driven commit path, which the leader's own first commit in the term triggers; the queued request is then served by the usual ReadOnlySafe path.
investigations.discriminator: Make a node win an election without any follower acknowledging its entry, submit a local ReadIndex while committedEntryInCurrentTerm is false, and record the queue size, the emitted heartbeats and the delivered read states; then deliver the replicated entry to the followers, step their acknowledgments back, and record whether the queued request is released and delivered with the new commit index. The same probe also submits a ReadIndex after that commit as the contrast path. If the queued request stays queued after the commit, or if it was answered before the commit, the hypothesis is refuted.

knowledge.assertion: The deferred path holds the request in pendingReadIndexMessages with no heartbeat and releases it through the MsgAppResp commit path, which is what the execution observed.

limitations: The probe submits the read request from the leader itself, so the delivered read state is the leader's own; a forwarded request from a follower would additionally exercise the MsgReadIndexResp path.

The leader is put into its pre-commit state by calling becomeCandidate/becomeLeader directly instead of waiting for an election round trip, because the intermediate state is otherwise not observable; the state itself is the library's normal post-election state.
Only the default ReadOnlySafe and a three-voter cluster are covered.

investigations.question: Can a client proposal that removes the last voter be accepted and committed by a single-voter cluster, and does applying the committed entry abort the applying node, or is the change rejected before it reaches the log?
investigations.hypothesis: The changer reports 'removed all voters' only when the configuration is computed at apply time, the leader's propose-time validation checks pending/joint state but not the resulting voter set, and raft.applyConfChange panics on any changer error, so a legal proposal can be accepted, committed, and then abort the applying node when the application applies it.
investigations.discriminator: On a single-voter leader, propose a ConfChangeV2 removing that voter through the real MsgProp path and record the returned error, whether the entry committed, and what happens when the documented application path applies it (panic recovered and reported verbatim); repeat with an add-voter change of the same shape as the control, which must apply without aborting. If the proposal is rejected before being appended, or if applying it returns an error instead of aborting, the hypothesis is refuted.

knowledge.assertion: The propose path does not check the resulting voter set and the apply path converts the changer's error into a panic, which is what the execution observed end to end.

limitations: The probe uses a single-voter cluster, which is the minimal configuration in which a proposable change removes the last voter; multi-voter removals that leave at least one voter are the control shape.

basis.prefix: Harness (draft file assurance_generated_test.go, package raft, execution package '.'; no captured file is replaced). assuranceCluster builds three real raft instances with newTestRaft(1|2|3, 10, 1, newTestMemoryStorage(withPeers(1,2,3))), wires them with newNetwork and elects node 1 by nt.send(MsgHup); it asserts r1.state == StateLeader and r1.committedEntryInCurrentTerm() and then clears the message queues. It emits a read_index_step (or prop_step) admission event carrying probe_id, role, entries, message type, node, term, log_committed and log_applied, then calls assuranceStepRecover, which steps the message and recovers any panic, and emits the outcome event with panicked, the verbatim recovered value, the number and types of emitted messages, and the target's state, term, pending/queue sizes and committed index after the step, followed by a probe_done event. result.summary: Draft updated at submission.json (validated read-only: valid, no diagnostics) with the harness assurance_generated_test.go; scratch removed. This turn opens one more input path on the proposal side: question @malformed_confchange_proposal with a sourced Behaviour entry and an experiment. Source trace: stepLeader unmarshals a proposal's conf-change payload and panics on a decode error (raft.go:1305-1313), while stepFollower relays a proposal by only rewriting m.To and sending it - it neither decodes the entries nor attaches a term (raft.go:1714-1724 with raft.go:536-541) - so an undecodable conf-change payload aborts whichever node decodes it and the relay hop neither rejects nor detects it. Three probes on freshly elected three-voter clusters, with panics recovered only in the harness: the malformed payload stepped directly into the leader, the same payload stepped into follower 2 and its forwarded message stepped into the leader, and a well-formed conf change of the same entry type as the control. Three comparisons encode the duties that a proposal the node cannot decode must be rejected rather than aborting it, and that relaying must not let the abort land on the leader (both expected violated), with the valid change (expected holds). Construction-time local runs show, for the record and not as formal evidence, the shape the experiment is built to measure: direct and forwarded malformed proposals both abort the leader with the verbatim decode error 'unexpected EOF' and leave the index unchanged, the forwarding follower neither panics nor refuses (one message to node 1), and the valid control is appended without aborting (index 1 to 2). Limitations state that the payload is a harness-constructed undecodable byte sequence, that the transport and admission layer are outside the captured package, that only the EntryConfChangeV2 variant was executed, and that reachability through a real peer is a question for human review; the formal conclusion awaits the controller's retained receipt.

investigations.question: On a stable leader using ReadOnlySafe, can a ReadIndex request that carries an rctx equal to one that is still pending complete, or is that request silently discarded so that its requester receives no read index answer while the cluster keeps making progress?
investigations.hypothesis: The leader keys pending read requests by the rctx string only, so a second admission carrying an equal rctx is dropped without recording its own request message; when the single status completes, the answer is addressed to the first admission's requester and no answer is ever produced for the second requester, even though the leader stays leader and keeps satisfying quorum heartbeat acknowledgments.
investigations.discriminator: Drive two real voters to forward ReadIndex messages with equal rctx to the leader before any quorum acknowledgment, then deliver the quorum ack and eight further heartbeat rounds with acks from both followers; count read index answers per requester while confirming the leader stays in StateLeader. Controls: the identical shape with distinct rctxes (both requesters must be answered) and a single requester retrying its own rctx (that requester must be answered), which separate a duplicate-rctx admission loss from a broken harness or a generally stalled leader.

knowledge.assertion: The second admission with an equal rctx is discarded, so the leader keeps exactly one pending status and one stored request message for the two admissions.
Completion answers only the stored first request message, so a discarded equal-rctx admission produces neither a MsgReadIndexResp nor a ReadState.

counterevidence: node.go:218-229 states that callers must not reuse an rctx and that the reuse restriction is only lifted starting with release-3.7, so the silent drop may be the documented behaviour of this release-3.6 revision rather than an implementation error; this draft reports the mechanism and the observed starvation, and leaves that classification to human review.

The same-requester retry case is answered: when one requester retries its own rctx while the status is pending, the single response is addressed to that requester, so the observed starvation requires a requester whose equal-rctx message is discarded because another requester was admitted first.

Existing test coverage (raft_test.go:1192-1222) exercises one unique rctx and only checks that the queue and pending map drain; node_test.go:196-241 forwards two equal rctxes from different nodes but asserts only that the messages are forwarded and never checks for read index answers.
limitations: Only ReadOnlySafe is exercised; ReadOnlyLeaseBased and the pendingReadIndexMessages path (a leader that has not yet committed an entry in its term) are out of scope for this experiment.
The observation window is eight leader heartbeat rounds with quorum acknowledgments in one process; it establishes repeated nonprogress under normal opportunities rather than an unbounded guarantee.
The requester-side application contract (matching ReadStates by RequestCtx) is read from node.go / rawnode.go rather than executed.

investigations.question: Can a MsgReadIndex with an empty Entries slice reach the leader's read-index producer and panic the node, or is the message rejected, dropped or validated before the producer dereferences Entries[0]?
investigations.hypothesis: MsgReadIndex is sent and forwarded without a term (raft.go:536-541 keeps the local-message treatment for MsgProp/MsgReadIndex), a follower forwards it unchanged to its leader while a leader passes it straight to sendMsgReadIndexResponse (raft.go:1759-1765, 1346-1363), and that producer dereferences m.Entries[0] in readOnly.addRequest and responseToReadIndexReq without checking the slice length; only MsgReadIndexResp has an entry-count check (raft.go:1766-1772) and only MsgProp has an explicit empty-entry panic (raft.go:1286-1289). The apparent mismatch is therefore that the same message shape is validated for the response direction and for proposals but not for the request direction entering the leader's producer.
investigations.discriminator: Step a MsgReadIndex carrying no Entries into a follower (expected: forwarded to its leader, raft.go:1759-1765) and into a leader (expected by this hypothesis: an index-out-of-range panic inside the read-index producer), then step a well-formed one-entry MsgReadIndex into the same node as a positive control. Use a recovering wrapper that records the recovered value plus the leader's state, term and readOnly queue/pending sizes at the moment of the panic, and compare with the empty-MsgProp path that panics deliberately. If the empty-Entries message is instead dropped, converted to an error or silently ignored, the hypothesis is refuted and the observed disposition is the finding.

knowledge.assertion: readOnly.addRequest uses m.Entries[0].Data as the request key, which is the unchecked access that aborts on an empty payload.
responseToReadIndexReq answers the stored request through req.Entries[0].Data, so the same unchecked premise exists on the completion path.

limitations: A malformed or forged peer message may be considered outside the trusted transport contract, so a panic here would be an availability/robustness question rather than a divergence from consensus; the question is registered to establish the actual behaviour first.

The node-to-transport boundary is not part of the captured package, so reachability through a real peer depends on what the embedding application forwards to Node.Step.

investigations.question: When a conf change proposal fails the leader's propose-time validation, the leader replaces the entry with an empty EntryNormal and appends it while returning no error: can the proposing caller distinguish a discarded configuration change from an accepted one through the proposal result, and what does the log carry instead?
investigations.hypothesis: The conversion at raft.go:1333 keeps the proposal accepted: appendEntry succeeds, the returned error stays nil, the proposed index receives a normal entry with no data, pendingConfIndex is deliberately left untouched so the failed change is not treated as pending, and the resulting ConfState never changes, so a caller that only inspects the proposal result (nil error, committed index) cannot tell that its membership change was dropped. The apparent mismatch is between the proposal API's success signal and the responsibility to establish that the requested configuration change was admitted.
investigations.discriminator: On a leader in a simple (non-joint) configuration, propose a ConfChangeV2 with no changes and record (i) the error returned by Step, (ii) the type and Data length of the entry appended at the proposed index, (iii) the ConfState before and after that entry is committed and applied, and (iv) whether a second conf change proposed while one is pending is converted in the same way. Run the same proposal with DisableConfChangeValidation enabled as the control that must bypass the conversion, and compare with a valid single-node conf change as the positive control that must reach the applied ConfState. If the proposal error or the applied entry type/ConfState turn out to carry the distinction, the hypothesis is refuted.
counterevidence: The conversion is deliberate in the captured source: it is guarded by !r.disableConfChangeValidation, preceded by an Infof line naming the failed check, and Config.DisableConfChangeValidation documents propose-time verification as a feature, so a reviewer may read the empty-normal-entry substitution as intended behaviour rather than a silent drop.

The applying application sees the entry type when it applies the log, so an embedding server can in principle detect that its conf change became a normal entry; the question is about the proposal result and about what the library, not the embedding, guarantees.
limitations: No execution has been run for this question yet; the hypothesis rests only on the captured producer and the configuration documentation.
The discriminator covers a simple configuration and the empty-change case; joint configurations, learner changes and removals are separate branches of the same validation block.
Client-visible membership semantics of an embedding application (for example etcd's conf-change waiters) are outside the captured package.

investigations.question: When a committed configuration change removes the current leader and Config.StepDownOnRemoval is false, does the cluster still reach a new leader, or does the ineligible leader keep the leadership role and its heartbeats reset every eligible voter so that no proposal can commit and no election can complete without external intervention?
investigations.hypothesis: switchToConfig keeps the leadership role for a node that is absent from the new configuration when step-down is not requested, stepLeader then drops every proposal because the leader has no progress entry, and tickHeartbeat keeps broadcasting heartbeats that reset every remaining voter's election timer, so the cluster can neither commit client writes nor elect a replacement; with StepDownOnRemoval=true the same applied change makes the node a follower and the remaining voters elect a new leader.
investigations.discriminator: Propose, replicate and apply a ConfChangeV2 that removes node 1 on a three-voter cluster, then tick every node for a fixed number of rounds with prompt message delivery and record node states, whether a new leader was elected, the last index and committed index, and the proposal errors on the leader and on a forwarding follower; repeat with StepDownOnRemoval=true as the control. Also probe the read path on the ineligible leader with one and then a quorum of acknowledgments from the current voters. If the ineligible leader is eventually replaced, or if the followers campaign despite the heartbeats, the hypothesis is refuted.
limitations: The harness drives timers by ticking each node once per round in a fixed order, which is a legitimate but synthetic schedule; a real deployment also has network and scheduling jitter.
The probe covers simple removal of the leader in a three-voter cluster; joint configurations, learner demotion and multi-node changes are not exercised.
Whether StepDownOnRemoval=false is the right default for an embedding service, and whether an operator is expected to intervene, is a contract question outside the captured package.

investigations.question: Does a ReadIndex request that reaches a leader before it has committed an entry in its current term get delivered once that first commit happens, or can it remain queued while the leader keeps making progress?

investigations.question: Can a client proposal that removes the last voter be accepted and committed by a single-voter cluster, and does applying the committed entry abort the applying node, or is the change rejected before it reaches the log?
investigations.hypothesis: The changer reports 'removed all voters' only when the configuration is computed at apply time, the leader's propose-time validation checks pending/joint state but not the resulting voter set, and raft.applyConfChange panics on any changer error, so a legal proposal can be accepted, committed, and then abort the applying node when the application applies it.
investigations.discriminator: On a single-voter leader, propose a ConfChangeV2 removing that voter through the real MsgProp path and record the returned error, whether the entry committed, and what happens when the documented application path applies it (panic recovered and reported verbatim); repeat with an add-voter change of the same shape as the control, which must apply without aborting. If the proposal is rejected before being appended, or if applying it returns an error instead of aborting, the hypothesis is refuted.

knowledge.assertion: The propose path does not check the resulting voter set and the apply path converts the changer's error into a panic, which is what the execution observed end to end.

limitations: The probe uses a single-voter cluster, which is the minimal configuration in which a proposable change removes the last voter; multi-voter removals that leave at least one voter are the control shape.
The harness recovers the panic itself; the process-level consequence and any restart behaviour are inferred from the panic rather than observed.

investigations.question: After a node applies a configuration that removes it, does a proposal made through the Node API report that the proposal cannot be admitted, or does the call block until the caller's context expires without any signal that the node is no longer a member?
investigations.hypothesis: node.run sets the proposal channel to nil when the node applies a removal of itself, and Node.Propose's wait path selects only on that channel, the caller's context and the node's done channel, so the call blocks and returns the caller's context error (or ErrStopped) rather than any statement about admissibility, even though the raft layer's own proposal path returns a drop error when the removed node is the leader.
investigations.discriminator: Drive a three-voter cluster with node 3 behind the Node API, make it a follower of a bare leader, propose through node 3's Node while it is still a member with a short-lived context (expected: returns promptly with no error), then remove node 3 on the leader, apply the committed entry on node 3, and repeat the same Node.Propose call with the same timeout, recording the returned error text and the elapsed time. If the second call returns a raft error before the deadline, the hypothesis is refuted.

knowledge.assertion: The proposal channel is disabled when the node applies its own removal, so the call can only complete on the caller's context, which is what the execution observed.

limitations: The probe uses a short-lived caller context; with a non-expiring context the call would block until the node stops, which the harness does not measure directly.
The removal is applied only on the subject node through the Node API while the other two voters are bare raft instances driven by the harness.
The embedding service's own proposal timeouts, retries and membership tracking are outside the captured package.

investigations.question: Does a proposal whose conf-change entry cannot be decoded abort the node that processes it, and does a follower's proposal-forwarding hop validate the payload before relaying it to the leader?
investigations.hypothesis: stepLeader decodes the conf-change payload of a proposal and panics on failure, stepFollower forwards a proposal without examining its entries and without attaching a term, so a proposal carrying an undecodable conf-change payload aborts whichever node decodes it, and relaying it through a follower only moves the abort to the leader without any rejection at the relay.

knowledge.statement: On the acknowledging heartbeat, stepLeader asks readOnly.advance for the statuses up to the acknowledged ctx and then answers each returned status through responseToReadIndexReq(rs.req, rs.index): a status whose stored request came from a remote peer produces one MsgReadIndexResp addressed to that stored request's From, and a status whose stored request came from the leader itself appends one local ReadState. knowledge.statement: When a node applies a configuration in which it was a member before and is absent from the new voters (and from VotersOutgoing), node.run disables its proposal channel by setting propc to nil; Node.Propose/ProposeConfChange reach that channel through stepWithWaitOption, whose select can complete only on the channel send, on ctx.Done or on n.done. A proposal issued after such an application therefore blocks and returns only the caller's context error or ErrStopped, and the raft step path that would otherwise run (a follower forwarding the MsgProp to its leader) is never invoked, so the library's own drop signal (raft.go:1290-1295 for the removed-leader case) is not produced on this path.
knowledge.conditions: The node is driven through the Node API with an asynchronous run loop, it applied a committed configuration that removed it while it was in the previous configuration, its proposal channel was therefore disabled, and the caller supplies a context with a deadline (a non-expiring context blocks until the node stops).

knowledge.statement: In the retained execution of the fixed experiment (three-voter cluster {1,2,3}; node 1 a bare raft leader at term 1 with committed 1, node 2 a bare follower, node 3 driven through the Node API as a follower; fault-free in-process delivery; caller timeout 200 ms), Node.Propose on node 3 while it was still a member returned no error in 0 ms (parsed index 1: error_text '<nil>', elapsed_ms 0, blocked_until_deadline false, node3_in_config true). After a ConfChangeV2 removing node 3 was proposed on the leader and applied on node 3 through the Node API, node 3 was absent from the configuration with voters [1,2] (index 2: node3_in_config false, node3_lead 1, node3_state StateFollower, committed 3), and the same Node.Propose call then blocked for 201 ms and returned only the caller's context error (index 3: error_text 'context deadline exceeded', elapsed_ms 201, timeout_ms 200, blocked_until_deadline true).
knowledge.conditions: One executed in-process experiment with the fixed harness bytes of experiment b8fa9bc20e164089beff30308ce68220-experiment (receipt d5f37430774c4bbd9d64967e3f82290d, exit 0, changed_target_files [], no parsing errors); the subject node was driven through the Node API with its own Ready/Advance loop, the other voters were bare raft instances, the caller used a 200 ms context, and no restart, snapshot, leadership change or packet loss occurred. One observed instance under these conditions, not a universal guarantee.

knowledge.statement: In the retained execution of the successor experiment (three-voter cluster {1,2,3}; node 1 a bare raft leader at term 1 with committed 1, node 2 a bare follower, node 3 driven through the Node API as a follower; fault-free in-process delivery), Node.Propose on node 3 while it was a member returned no error in 0 ms (parsed index 1: error_text '<nil>', elapsed_ms 0, blocked_until_deadline false, node3_in_config true). After node 3 applied a ConfChangeV2 that removed it (index 2: node3_in_config false, voters [1,2], committed 3), a proposal with a 200 ms deadline blocked for the whole deadline and returned 'context deadline exceeded' (index 3: elapsed_ms 200, blocked_until_deadline true). A proposal issued with context.Background from a separate goroutine did not return during the fixed 300 ms observation window (index 4: returned_within_window false, error_text '<nil>', node3_in_config false), and it returned only after the node was stopped, with the error text 'raft: stopped' (index 5: returned_after_stop true).
knowledge.conditions: One executed in-process experiment with the fixed harness bytes of experiment 34e68e30368140d492185254dcedf04b-experiment (receipt 133c591601724c759fe07b2e80b55649, exit 0, changed_target_files [], no parsing errors); the subject node was driven through the Node API with its own Ready/Advance loop, the other voters were bare raft instances, the removal was proposed on the leader and applied on the subject node, no restart, snapshot or leadership change occurred, and the witness call was observed for 300 ms before the node was stopped. One observed instance under these conditions, not a universal guarantee.

knowledge.statement: In stepLeader, a MsgProp whose entry type is EntryConfChange or EntryConfChangeV2 is unmarshalled into the corresponding conf-change struct and any decode error panics the node processing the proposal (raft.go:1305-1313); nothing earlier on the path inspects the payload, because stepFollower relays a proposal by only rewriting m.To and sending it, without attaching a term or decoding the entries (raft.go:1714-1724 with raft.go:536-541). A proposal carrying an undecodable conf-change payload therefore aborts whichever node decodes it, and the follower that relays it neither rejects nor detects the problem.
knowledge.conditions: The receiver is a leader in the middle of handling MsgProp (for example a freshly elected leader in a three-voter configuration), the proposal is delivered either directly or through a follower that forwards proposals to its leader, and the entry type is a conf-change type with a payload that fails the library's protobuf decode.

scope.description: In-process three-voter cluster (nodes 1, 2, 3 of the captured raft package, one process, three real state machines), ReadOnlySafe, fault-free delivery, no proposal, no election after node 1 becomes leader, no snapshot and no membership change. The requested question is only whether each admitted ReadIndex request receives a read index answer.
assumptions: ReadOnlyOption is the default ReadOnlySafe for newTestRaft.
Delivery is reliable and ordered as the harness steps messages explicitly; no network loss or reordering is injected.
Node 1 has committed an entry in its term before the read requests arrive, so stepLeader serves MsgReadIndex immediately instead of appending to pendingReadIndexMessages.
The two requester nodes chose byte-equal rctx values; only the requester identity and the rctx equality differ from the control scenario.
The leader remains leader during the observation window (verified in the emitted events).
excluded: ReadOnlyLeaseBased and lease-based reads
MsgReadIndex arriving before the leader has committed an entry in its term (pendingReadIndexMessages path)
leadership transfer, conf change, joint configuration, snapshot restore and restart
msg application / state machine reads beyond the raft ReadState and MsgReadIndexResp contract

basis.prefix: Initialization and producers in the draft harness (draft file assurance_generated_test.go, package raft, execution package '.'; no captured file is replaced). assuranceCluster builds three real raft instances with newTestRaft(1|2|3, 10, 1, newTestMemoryStorage(withPeers(1,2,3))), wires them with newNetwork and elects node 1 by nt.send(MsgHup); it asserts r1.state == StateLeader and r1.committedEntryInCurrentTerm() before clearing all message queues. assuranceForward uses the real caller path: Step a local MsgReadIndex{From:id,To:id,Type:MsgReadIndex,Entries:[{Data:rctx}]} into follower f and take the single forwarded MsgReadIndex (stepFollower sets m.To = f.lead without attaching a term), then Step that message into the leader. Scenario duplicate_ctx: follower 2 forwards rctx 'assurance-dup-rctx' and the leader steps it; follower 3 then forwards the same rctx and the leader steps it while the first status is still pending; a third identical retry from follower 3 is also stepped. The leader then receives MsgHeartbeatResp{From:2,Context:rctx} (quorum of voters {1,2,3} is reached by the leader's own ack plus node 2) plus eight further rounds of MsgHeartbeatResp from nodes 3 and 2 followed by leader.tickHeartbeat(); every emitted message is inspected for MsgReadIndexResp and counted per destination. Scenario distinct_ctx repeats exactly the same sequence with two different rctx values, and scenario same_requester_retry repeats it with a single follower retrying its own rctx. Events record, per admission, the pending/queue sizes after the admission; per retry, the queue change and emitted heartbeats; per round, the leader state, pending/queue sizes and cumulative responses per requester; and per request, the final responded flag, response count, awaited rounds and the requester's ReadState count.
basis.responsibility: The leader-side ReadIndex producer owns producing a read index answer (one local ReadState for a local request, or one MsgReadIndexResp to the requesting peer) for every ReadIndex request it admits; the documented caller contract states that lost ReadIndex requests are the caller's to retry and that reusing an rctx is supported from release-3.7 on.

comparisons.description: Admitted ReadIndex requests that carry an rctx equal to another requester's pending rctx each receive a read index answer.
Control: with identical timing and distinct rctxes, each admitted ReadIndex request receives a read index answer.
Control: a single requester retrying its own pending rctx still receives a read index answer for that rctx.

scope.description: In-process three-voter cluster (nodes 1, 2, 3 of the captured raft package, three real state machines per probe, a freshly elected leader per probe) with the default ReadOnlySafe option. Each probe feeds one message through the real Step entry point of the addressed node and records what the state machine did, including a panic recovered by the harness.
assumptions: MsgReadIndex and MsgProp shapes that a peer could deliver are represented by constructing the pb.Message directly and stepping it into the addressed node; the harness replicates what the captured library would receive from a transport.
The leader has committed an entry in its term before the probes, so the read-index producer is reached directly instead of appending to pendingReadIndexMessages.
Delivery is fault-free and in-process; no network, snapshot, membership or restart event is injected.
The panic is recovered only by the harness. In production the same panic escapes (*raft).Step and aborts the caller's raft loop, which is why the recovered value is reported verbatim.
excluded: The embedding application's transport and message validation, which is outside the captured package
Byzantine peers, admission control and message authentication
ReadOnlyLeaseBased, pendingReadIndexMessages, membership change and leader change
Any state-machine effect of a proposal, since the probes carry either no payload or one payload and are not applied

basis.prefix: Harness (draft file assurance_generated_test.go, package raft, execution package '.'; no captured file is replaced). assuranceCluster builds three real raft instances with newTestRaft(1|2|3, 10, 1, newTestMemoryStorage(withPeers(1,2,3))), wires them with newNetwork and elects node 1 by nt.send(MsgHup); it asserts r1.state == StateLeader and r1.committedEntryInCurrentTerm() and then clears the message queues. For each probe the harness builds a fresh cluster, selects the target node (the leader for role 'leader', follower 2 for role 'follower'), emits a probe_setup event with the target's term and state, and constructs pb.Message{From: target.id, To: target.id, Type: MsgReadIndex or MsgProp, Entries: payload} where payload is empty or holds one entry. It emits a read_index_step (or prop_step) admission event carrying probe_id, role, entries, message type, node, term, log_committed and log_applied, then calls assuranceStepRecover, which steps the message and recovers any panic, and emits the outcome event with panicked, the verbatim recovered value, the number and types of emitted messages, and the target's state, term, pending/queue sizes and committed index after the step, followed by a probe_done event. Probes: 'leader/empty-entries' (MsgReadIndex, no Entries) is expected to panic, 'leader/one-entry' (MsgReadIndex, one entry) is the positive control expected to emit heartbeats and create one pending status, 'leader/empty-prop' (MsgProp, no Entries) is the guarded contrast expected to panic with the library's own message, 'follower/empty-entries' and 'follower/one-entry' are expected to forward exactly one MsgReadIndex to the leader. The test asserts these observed outcomes so that a behaviour change fails the test instead of reshaping the evidence.
basis.responsibility: A node that processes a message delivered to it by a peer must not abort the process because of that message's shape: it must reject, drop or otherwise handle the shape. The captured library makes that choice explicitly for proposals (MsgProp with no entries panics deliberately) and validates the entry count for MsgReadIndexResp, so the same duty applies to the MsgReadIndex path that enters the leader's read-index producer.

comparisons.description: Stepping a MsgReadIndex with no Entries into a leader does not panic the node.
Control: stepping a well-formed MsgReadIndex with one entry into a leader does not panic the node.
Control: stepping the same read-index shapes into a follower does not panic the node.
Contrast: an empty MsgProp panics deliberately with the library's own guard message.

scope.description: Four in-process probes on freshly elected three-voter clusters (nodes 1, 2, 3 of the captured raft package) with the leader in a simple non-joint configuration and everything committed already applied. Each probe proposes one or two conf changes through the real MsgProp path and observes the returned error, the appended entry at the proposed index, pendingConfIndex, and the configuration reached by the application's type-based apply loop.
assumptions: The harness also plays the embedding application: after election it advances the applied index past the leader's committed index, as an application does after applying committed entries, so the propose-time check 'alreadyPending' does not fire for the first proposal.

Proposals are represented as pb.Message{Type: MsgProp, Entries: [{Type: EntryConfChangeV2, Data: marshalled ConfChangeV2}]} stepped into the leader, which is the shape Node.ProposeConfChange delivers.

The apply emulation follows the documented application duty: for the entry at the proposed index, ApplyConfChange is invoked only when the entry type is EntryConfChange or EntryConfChangeV2, and any panic from that call is recovered and reported as an operand.
The pending-case probe's second proposal carries a valid single-node change so that its fate is decided by the pending check rather than by the payload.
Delivery is fault-free and in-process; no restart, snapshot, joint configuration or leader change is injected.
excluded: Joint configurations and leave-joint transitions
Learner changes, removals and multi-node atomic changes
The embedding application's own conf-change waiters and client-visible membership APIs
Persistence, restart and snapshot interactions

basis.prefix: Harness (draft file assurance_generated_test.go, package raft, execution package '.'; no captured file is replaced). assuranceClusterWithConfig builds the three-voter cluster through newNetworkWithConfig with a configFunc that sets Config.DisableConfChangeValidation for the bypass probe, elects node 1 by nt.send(MsgHup), asserts StateLeader, and then performs the application duty r1.appliedTo(r1.raftLog.committed, 0) so the leader's applied index covers its committed entries. Each probe then: emits a conf_change_step admission event with proposal_id, scenario, validation_enabled, leader, term, state, committed_before, applied_before, pending_conf_index and voters_before; marshals the ConfChangeV2, steps one MsgProp carrying it into the leader, records the returned error text, takes the appended entry at the new last index via raftLog.slice and records its type and data length, records pendingConfIndex after the step, and for the pending probe repeats the same measurement for a second proposal. It then drives the messages the state machines produced (leader bcastAppend, follower MsgAppResp and any further messages) through a bounded queue until the cluster quiesces, records whether the first proposed index became committed, and runs the type-based apply loop for that entry (ApplyConfChange only for conf-change entry types, with panics recovered), recording the voters and whether the configuration changed. Finally it emits a conf_change_proposal result event with error_reported/error_text, entry_type, entry_data_len, proposed_index, pending_conf_index_after, pending_conf_index_set, outcome_class computed as 'rejected' if an error was reported, else 'admitted' if the entry type is EntryConfChange or EntryConfChangeV2, else 'silently_replaced', plus committed, applied_conf_state_changed, apply_panicked/apply_error, conf_state_voters_after and leader_state; the pending probe additionally reports the same operands for its second proposal as second_* fields including second_outcome_class. The test asserts the positive control (valid addition must commit and change the configuration) so that a harness or cluster failure cannot be mistaken for the measured outcome.
basis.responsibility: The leader's proposal path owns telling the caller whether the requested configuration change was admitted: either the entry keeps a conf-change payload and reaches ApplyConfChange, or the call reports an error. Substituting an unrelated empty normal entry while returning success leaves the caller unable to distinguish a dropped membership change from an accepted one using the proposal result alone.

comparisons.description: A conf change that fails propose-time validation in a simple configuration is not silently replaced by an unrelated empty normal entry without an error.
A second conf change proposed while an earlier one is still unapplied is not silently replaced by an unrelated empty normal entry without an error.
Control: with DisableConfChangeValidation the same empty change keeps its conf-change payload and is not replaced.
Positive control: a valid single-node addition is admitted, commits and reaches the applied configuration.

scope.description: Two probes on freshly elected three-voter clusters. Each probe proposes and replicates a ConfChangeV2 removing node 1, applies that committed entry on all three nodes with the documented type-based application loop, advances each node's applied index, verifies that node 1 is no longer in the configuration, then runs a fixed 80-round progress window in which every node is ticked once per round and all produced messages are delivered promptly, and finally probes the read path on the ineligible leader.
assumptions: The removal is proposed and replicated by the real producer path (MsgProp with an EntryConfChangeV2 payload, then the actual MsgApp/MsgAppResp exchange) and is applied only after it is committed.

The harness plays the application duties: type-based ApplyConfChange for conf-change entries and advancing the applied index up to the committed index, which a real application does through its Ready/Advance loop.

Election and heartbeat timers are driven by ticking each node once per round in a fixed order with messages delivered immediately after each tick, so a candidate's vote request reaches its peer before that peer's next tick.
Delivery is fault-free and in-process; no restart, snapshot, partition or external client is involved.
The initial configuration is {1,2,3}; after the removal it is {2,3} with quorum 2, and node 1 is a non-voter.
excluded: Joint configurations, learners and multi-node atomic changes
The embedding application's membership controller and any operator intervention
ReadOnlyLeaseBased, snapshots, restarts and persistence faults
Byzantine or network-fault scenarios

basis.prefix: Harness (draft file assurance_generated_test.go, package raft, execution package '.'; no captured file is replaced). assuranceClusterWithConfig builds {1,2,3} through newNetworkWithConfig so the step-down control runs through the real Config, elects node 1 by nt.send(MsgHup), asserts StateLeader and advances the applied index. Each probe then marshals ConfChangeV2{Changes:[{Type: RemoveNode, NodeID: 1}]}, steps one MsgProp carrying it into the leader, drives the produced messages through a bounded queue until the cluster quiesces, and checks that the proposed index is committed. Every node whose committed index covers that entry runs the documented type-based application loop (ApplyConfChange for conf-change entries, panics recovered) and then advances its applied index to its committed index. The probe emits removal_applied with the proposal error, proposed index, whether the removal committed, the leader's state, whether node 1 is still in the configuration, the voters, and all node states; then a progress_setup admission event with probe_id, step_down_on_removal, ticks, leader state and configuration membership; then it issues one proposal on the leader and one on follower 2 (whose forwarding is delivered to the leader) and records both errors plus the forwarded message type and destination. The progress window ticks each node once per round in a fixed order, delivering each node's produced messages immediately, for 80 rounds, and emits progress_window with the proposal errors, forwarding operands, last index and committed index before/after, all node states, the set of nodes that hold leadership, whether a new leader was elected, the followers' election timers, and any undelivered messages. On the ineligible-leader probe it then forwards a ReadIndex from follower 2 into the leader, delivers the resulting heartbeats to the real followers, steps exactly one of their acknowledgments and records the answers, then steps the remaining acknowledgment and records the answers, emitting two removed_leader_read events with acks_from_current_voters, read_answers, leader state and voters.
basis.responsibility: A cluster whose configuration no longer contains its current leader owns reaching a configuration-consistent leader so that client writes can commit again. Keeping an ineligible node in the leadership role while its heartbeats keep every eligible voter's election timer reset leaves the cluster unable to commit anything and unable to elect a replacement without external intervention.

comparisons.description: With StepDownOnRemoval false, a cluster whose configuration no longer contains the current leader elects a new leader within the fixed progress window.
Control: with StepDownOnRemoval true, the same sequence elects a new leader within the same progress window.

scope.description: Two probes on freshly elected three-voter clusters with the default ReadOnlySafe. Each probe admits two ReadIndex requests from follower 2, commits one write between them through the real MsgProp/MsgApp/MsgAppResp exchange, then delivers the real followers' heartbeat acknowledgments and records the index carried by the answer for the second request's rctx.
assumptions: Follower 2 issues each ReadIndex through its own Step and the harness forwards the produced MsgReadIndex to the leader, which is the real caller path.

The heartbeats the leader broadcasts at the first admission are held back and delivered only after the write is committed and the second admission happened, so the first status stays pending across both admissions.
The write is a normal proposal replicated by the real leader and acknowledged by the real followers; the harness only transports messages.
The derived field answer_index_at_least_admission is computed as answer_index >= committed_at_second_admission and both operands are reported.
Delivery is fault-free and in-process; no restart, snapshot, membership change or leadership change occurs.
excluded: ReadOnlyLeaseBased and the pendingReadIndexMessages path
Application-level matching of ReadStates by RequestCtx beyond what node.go documents
Network faults, restarts, membership changes and joint configurations

basis.prefix: Harness (draft file assurance_generated_test.go, package raft, execution package '.'; no captured file is replaced). assuranceCluster builds {1,2,3}, elects node 1 and clears its queues. Each probe then: (1) makes follower 2 Step a local MsgReadIndex with rctx X, takes the single forwarded MsgReadIndex and Steps it into the leader, records the emitted heartbeats (which carry rctx X) into heldHeartbeats and emits read_index_admission for request_id 'first' with committed_at_admission, pending_after and queue_after; (2) proposes one write on the leader, drives only the messages produced from that point through a bounded queue until the write is committed, so the held heartbeats stay undelivered and the first read status stays pending while the leader's committed index advances; (3) makes follower 2 Step a second ReadIndex whose rctx is either equal to X (probe reuse-rctx) or different (probe distinct-rctx), forwards it, records the newly emitted heartbeats and emits read_index_admission for request_id 'second' with its own committed_at_admission, pending_after and queue_after; (4) delivers all held and newly produced heartbeats to the real followers, collects the acknowledgments they produce, steps them into the leader and records every MsgReadIndexResp, keyed by the rctx it carries. Finally it emits read_index_answer for request_id 'second' with rctx, committed_at_first_admission, committed_after_write, committed_at_second_admission, answer_index (the index of the answer carrying the second request's rctx), answers (total answers), the derived answer_index_at_least_admission, and the leader state. The test asserts the observed behaviour in both probes so a change in either direction fails the harness instead of silently reshaping the evidence.
basis.responsibility: The leader-side read-index producer owns associating each admitted read request with a read index that is at least as new as the commit index the leader had when that request was admitted; a caller that retries or reuses an rctx must not be answered with an index recorded for an earlier admission.

comparisons.description: With a reused rctx, the answer carrying that rctx has an index at least as new as the commit index at the second admission.
Control: with distinct rctxes the second admission's answer carries an index at least as new as its own admission-time commit index.

scope.description: One probe on a freshly built three-voter cluster whose node 1 is made leader without any follower acknowledgment, so it has no committed entry in its term. The probe submits a local ReadIndex, observes the queue, then delivers the replication messages and the followers' acknowledgments to drive the first commit, and finally submits a second ReadIndex after that commit as the contrast path.
assumptions: The leader is made to win directly (becomeCandidate + becomeLeader) so that the pre-commit state is observable; this is the same state the library reaches momentarily after a real election.
Read requests are submitted locally by the leader, which steps a MsgReadIndex exactly as Node.ReadIndex does.
All messages are delivered in process with no loss, and the followers are ordinary fresh raft instances configured with the same voter set.
The default ReadOnlySafe option is used, so an answer requires the leader's own acknowledgment plus a quorum of voter acknowledgments produced by the real followers.
excluded: ReadOnlyLeaseBased and forwarded read requests from followers
Snapshots, restarts, membership changes, leadership changes and network faults
Any application-level interpretation of the delivered read state

basis.prefix: Harness (draft file assurance_generated_test.go, package raft, execution package '.'; no captured file is replaced). The test builds three real raft instances with newTestRaft(1|2|3, 10, 1, newTestMemoryStorage(withPeers(1,2,3))), calls r1.becomeCandidate() and r1.becomeLeader() so that node 1 leads with an uncommitted entry in its term, and takes r1.bcastAppend()'s messages while recording committedEntryInCurrentTerm() (expected false). Next it delivers the leader's MsgApp to nodes 2 and 3 through a bounded queue, steps the MsgAppResp acknowledgments they produce back into the leader, and emits read_index_released with the new committed index, committed_in_term, queued_after, read_states_after, delivered, read_state_index, undelivered_messages and leader state. basis.responsibility: The leader-side ReadIndex producer owns eventually answering a read request that it accepted for later processing: a request that the leader deferred because it had no committed entry in its term must be released by the commit that makes the read index available, not left waiting for an unrelated later proposal.

comparisons.description: A ReadIndex request deferred before the leader's first commit in its term is delivered once that commit happens.

scope.description: Two probes on freshly elected three-voter clusters, each proposing, replicating and applying a ConfChangeV2 that removes node 1, running a fixed 80-round progress window with round-robin ticking and prompt delivery, probing the read path on the ineligible leader, and then, for the probe without step-down, letting an eligible voter campaign explicitly and proposing on the resulting leader.
assumptions: The removal is proposed and replicated by the real producer path and applied only after it is committed, with each node's applied index advanced as an application does.
Timers are driven by ticking each node once per round in a fixed order with messages delivered immediately after each tick.

The external trigger is one MsgHup stepped into follower 2, which is the same message Node.Campaign and a forced election use; the harness then proposes one write on whichever eligible node becomes leader.
Delivery is fault-free and in-process; no restart, snapshot, partition, joint configuration or operator-side membership change is simulated.

Network faults, restarts and snapshots
The embedding application's membership controller and its operator interfaces
Any claim about how quickly an operator would notice or act in a real deployment
